+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+

# Submission Metadata

## Journal

Journal of Number Theory

## Title

Arithmetic Criticality and Large Deviations for Fibonacci Partitions and
Finite-Window Fibers

## Authors

- Haobo Ma, AELF PTE LTD., Singapore
- Wenlin Zhang, National University of Singapore, Singapore

## 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification

11B39, 05A17, 60F10

## Keywords

Fibonacci partition function; Erdos measure; Bernoulli convolution;
Zeckendorf representation; large deviations

## Summary

The manuscript studies the Fibonacci partition function and an exact
finite-window Zeckendorf fold. It identifies the arithmetic critical parameter
by

\[
\frac{\zeta(\sigma_0-1)}{\zeta(\sigma_0)}=2,
\]

proves the low-temperature denominator-layer asymptotic with its explicit
one-large-partial-quotient context sum, and derives the critical cost tail and
the second-order \(m^{3-\sigma_0}\) corrections beyond the leading constants
\(2/\mu_C\) and \(4/\mu_C\). It also proves uniform coexistence limits and
finite-layer large deviations at nonexposed slopes, and establishes exact
finite-window fiber identities. On
each fixed finite prime support it retains an exact rational coefficient
generating function. It asserts no directional coefficient asymptotic and no
quenched-velocity asymptotic.

## Relation To Prior Results

Sidorov and Vershik use \(F^{\mathrm{SV}}_1=1\) and
\(F^{\mathrm{SV}}_2=2\), so their indexing is

\[
F^{\mathrm{SV}}_j=F_{j+1}.
\]

Their finite representation frequency \(f_m(k)\) is therefore the same raw
finite Fibonacci subset-sum coefficient used in the manuscript, after this
index shift, and \(2^{-m}f_m(k)\) gives the finite masses approximating the
Erdos measure. Hu treated local dimensions of the golden-ratio Bernoulli
convolution. Lau and Ngai determined its positive-\(q\) \(L^q\)-spectrum.
Feng--Olivier and Feng determined the all-real spectrum and its negative
first-order phase transition.

With

\[
\tau_\mu(t)=\lim\frac{\log\sum_I\mu(I)^t}{\log|I|},
\]

the exact normalization used throughout the submission is

\[
P(t)=t\log 2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
\]

Accordingly, the all-real pressure formula and the frozen negative branch are
recorded as attributed recovery and consistency results. The surviving
contributions are the arithmetic evaluation of the critical point, the
one-sided critical moment, the local denominator-layer theorem and explicit
context constant, the stable second-order critical finite-size laws and
coexistence laws, the finite-layer nonexposed-slope lower bounds, and the
exact finite-window correspondences and identities.

## Exact Scope Of Finite Formulas

The affine fiber--partition correspondence and partition-difference formula
hold for every integer \(m\ge 1\). The two-interval fiber identity itself is
stated for \(m\ge 0\).

\end{cases}
\]

is defined only for \(k\ge 5\). The even-index quantities

\begin{cases}
G_{k+2}G_{k-5}+G_3+1,&k\text{ even},\\

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+

Moshchevitin--Zhigljavsky studied global entropies of Farey-tree partitions
\cite{MoshchevitinZhigljavsky2004}.  In that line, Dushistova introduced the
same fixed-digit-sum continuant sum that occurs here and stated a fuller
asymptotic expansion \cite[Thm.~3]{Dushistova2007}.  Her printed leading
coefficient, translated to the notation below, is \(R_s+2R_s^2\).  The
term-by-term identification and the endpoint correction giving \(2R_s^2\)
are recorded after the theorem statement; the correction concerns the
leading coefficient in that theorem, not the other results of her paper.

\begin{theorem}[Corrected denominator-layer asymptotic]
\label{thm:arithmetic-denominator-layer}
For a finite word \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\) of positive integers, let
\(\mathcal K(\mathbf a)\) be its regular continuant, with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
  \mathcal K(\varnothing)=1,\qquad \mathcal K(a_1)=a_1,\\
  \mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_r)
  =a_r\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_{r-1})
   +\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_{r-2}).
 \end{gathered}
\]
Put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
  \mathcal C_{\rm L}&:=\{\varnothing\}\cup
   \bigcup_{r\ge1}\mathbb N^r,\\
  \mathcal C_{\rm R}&:=\{\varnothing\}\cup
   \{(a_1,\ldots,a_r):r\ge1,\ a_i\ge1,\ a_r\ge2\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Then, for every fixed \(s>2\),
\begin{equation}
 b_{2d+1}(s)\sim b(s)d^{-s}\qquad(d\to\infty),
 \label{eq:low-temperature-local-layer}
\end{equation}
where the constant is the absolutely convergent one-large-partial-quotient
context sum
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 b(s)
 &: =\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
       \sum_{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}}
       \{\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)\}^{-s}\\
 &=2\left(\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)}\right)^2>0.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:one-large-partial-quotient-context-sum}
\end{equation}
This is a corrected form, with a simplified context proof, of the leading
term in Dushistova's expansion.  No tail hypothesis is used in
\eqref{eq:low-temperature-local-layer}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
\[
 \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
 \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
 a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
 \qquad
 \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
\]
Then, term by term,
\begin{equation}
 b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
 \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
 \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
is
\[
 [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
\]
and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
even \(t\),
\[
 (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
\]
where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
negative digit gives in all three cases
\[
 d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
\]
Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
For \(s>2\), put
\[
 r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
 \qquad
 \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
\]
Then
\[
 r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
 \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
\]
Consequently, if
\[
 R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
\]
the three left-context cases contribute respectively
\begin{equation}
\begin{array}{c|c}
 |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
 |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
 |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
\end{array}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
 \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
\end{equation}
At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
proves all four identities and the three contributions in
\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.

The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
For \(s>2\), define
\[
 \eta_s(h):=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
\]
and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
\begin{equation}
 G_s(N,h)\le
 \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
 \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
 \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
 \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Write \(|\mathbf a|_1=a_1+\cdots+a_r\), with
\(|\varnothing|_1=0\).  The canonical regular continued fraction of a reduced
\(p/q\in(0,1)\) is
\[
 \frac pq=[0;a_1,\ldots,a_r],
 \qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_r\ge2,
\]
and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\).  By the termwise
conversion in \Cref{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}, on putting
\(n=d+1\), the left side of \eqref{eq:low-temperature-local-layer} is
\begin{equation}
 A_n(s):=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf a\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\|\mathbf a|_1=n}}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-s}.
 \label{eq:regular-continuant-layer}
\end{equation}

The context evaluation in \Cref{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction} gives,
for \(s>2\),
\begin{equation}
 R_s:=\sum_{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}}\mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s}
 =1+\sum_{q\ge2}\frac{\phi_{\rm E}(q)}{q^s}
 =\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)}<\infty.
 \label{eq:right-continuant-context-mass}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
 L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}\mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
 =2R_s.
 \label{eq:left-continuant-context-mass}
\end{equation}
This proves the absolute convergence and the evaluation in
\eqref{eq:one-large-partial-quotient-context-sum}.

It remains to prove that this context sum is the whole local main term.  We
give the cutoff argument, including the multiple-large-digit and moderate
parts.  The continuant concatenation formula implies, for finite positive
words \(\mathbf u,\mathbf v\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf u\mathbf v)
 \ge \mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v).
 \label{eq:continuant-concatenation-lower-bound}
\end{equation}
Moreover, with the two contexts fixed and \(a\to\infty\), multilinearity of
the tridiagonal determinant defining the continuant gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K(\mathbf u,a,\mathbf v)
 =a\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)+O_{\mathbf u,\mathbf v}(1).
 \label{eq:continuant-large-digit-affine}
\end{equation}

Let \(P_n(s)\) be the part of \eqref{eq:regular-continuant-layer} coming from
words having a digit greater than \(n/2\).  Such a digit is unique.  Cutting
there is a bijection with pairs
\((\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\times\mathcal C_{\rm R}\)
satisfying
\(|\mathbf u|_1+|\mathbf v|_1<n/2\), the middle digit being

 succeeded in 258ms:
\(a=n-|\mathbf u|_1-|\mathbf v|_1\).  If \(\mathbf v\ne\varnothing\), its
final digit remains at least two; if \(\mathbf v=\varnothing\), then
\(a>n/2\), and for \(n\ge3\) the concatenated word is still canonical.
Thus, on the fixed countable context space,
\[
 n^sP_n(s)=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
 \sum_{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}}
 \mathbf 1_{\{|\mathbf u|_1+|\mathbf v|_1<n/2\}}
 \frac{n^s}{\mathcal K(\mathbf u,
 n-|\mathbf u|_1-|\mathbf v|_1,\mathbf v)^s}.
\]
Equations
\eqref{eq:continuant-concatenation-lower-bound} and
\eqref{eq:continuant-large-digit-affine} give, respectively,
\[
 n^s\mathcal K(\mathbf u,a,\mathbf v)^{-s}
 \le 2^s\{\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)\}^{-s}
\]
and pointwise convergence of the left side to
\(\{\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)\}^{-s}\).  Dominated
convergence, using \eqref{eq:right-continuant-context-mass}--
\eqref{eq:left-continuant-context-mass}, therefore yields
\begin{equation}
 n^sP_n(s)\longrightarrow L_sR_s=b(s).
 \label{eq:principal-large-digit-limit}
\end{equation}

We now show that the complementary words have total weight \(o(n^{-s})\).
Choose
\begin{equation}
 \frac{s}{2(s-1)}<\delta<1,
 \qquad h=\lfloor n^\delta\rfloor,
 \label{eq:large-digit-cutoff}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:left-continuant-context-mass}, \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).  A word having
at least two digits not smaller than \(h\) can be cut at its first two such
digits.  After dropping the restrictions on the three intervening contexts,
\eqref{eq:continuant-concatenation-lower-bound} bounds its total weight by
\begin{equation}
 L_s^2R_s
 \left(\sum_{a\ge h}a^{-s}\right)^2
 =O_s(h^{2-2s})=o(n^{-s}),
 \label{eq:two-large-digits-negligible}
\end{equation}
where the last equality is precisely the first inequality in
\eqref{eq:large-digit-cutoff}.

For words all of whose digits are smaller than \(h\),
\Cref{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound} applies.  When \(N\ge n/4\), its bound is
\(o(n^{-A})\) for every fixed \(A>0\), because \(n/h\to\infty\) and
\(\eta_s(h)\to0\).

The words not counted by \(P_n(s)\) and not covered by
\eqref{eq:two-large-digits-negligible} have at most one digit at least \(h\).
If there is none, apply \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound} with \(N=n\).  If
there is exactly one, its value is at most \(n/2\), so the two surrounding
moderate contexts have combined digit sum at least \(n/2\); one has digit sum
at least \(n/4\).  Cutting at the exceptional digit, bounding the short
context by \(L_s\), and allowing either context to be the long one gives the
explicit upper bound
\[
 2L_s\sum_{h\le a\le n/2}a^{-s}G_s(n/4,h).
\]
The first two factors grow at most polynomially, while the last is
superpolynomially small by \Cref{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}; hence this
is \(o(n^{-A})\) for every fixed \(A\).  Together with
\eqref{eq:two-large-digits-negligible}, this proves
\[
 A_n(s)-P_n(s)=o(n^{-s}).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:principal-large-digit-limit}, and replacing
\(n=d+1\) by \(d\), proves \eqref{eq:low-temperature-local-layer}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic critical stable renewal]
\label{thm:arithmetic-critical-stable-renewal}
Put \(\alpha:=\sigma_0-1\in(1,2)\), and under the critical letter law put
\[
 \Pr\{(C,H)=(c(p/q),\log q)\}=q^{-\sigma_0}.
\]
Then \(\Pr\{C=2d+1\}=b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)\), and the explicit constants
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 b_C&:=
 \sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
 \sum_{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}}
 \{\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)\}^{-\sigma_0}
 =2\left(\frac{\zeta(\sigma_0-1)}{\zeta(\sigma_0)}\right)^2=8,\\
 K_C&:=\frac{2^{\sigma_0-1}}{\sigma_0-1}b_C
 =\frac{2^{\sigma_0+2}}{\sigma_0-1}
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:critical-tail-constants}
\end{equation}
are positive.  The double series defining \(b_C\) is absolutely convergent,
and
\begin{align}
 b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)&\sim b_Cd^{-\sigma_0},
 &&d\to\infty,
 \label{eq:critical-letter-local-tail}\\
 \Pr\{C>x\}
 &=\sum_{q\ge2}q^{-\sigma_0}
   \card{\{1\le p<q:(p,q)=1,\ c(p/q)>x\}},\notag\\
 &\sim K_Cx^{1-\sigma_0},
 &&x\to\infty.
 \label{eq:critical-letter-tail}
\end{align}
If \(u_j=u_j(\sigma_0)\) is the renewal sequence in
\eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-coefficients}, then
\begin{equation}
 u_j=\frac1{\mu_C}
 +\frac{K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)}j^{2-\sigma_0}
 +o(j^{2-\sigma_0}).
 \label{eq:critical-renewal-second-order}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 Z_m^R(-\sigma_0)
 &=\frac{2m}{\mu_C}
 +\frac{2K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)(3-\sigma_0)}
   m^{3-\sigma_0}+o(m^{3-\sigma_0}),
 \label{eq:standard-layer-critical-second-order}\\
 S_{-\sigma_0}(m)
 &=\frac{4m}{\mu_C}
 +\frac{4K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)(3-\sigma_0)}
   m^{3-\sigma_0}+o(m^{3-\sigma_0}).
 \label{eq:finite-window-critical-second-order}
\end{align}
Finally, \(C\) belongs to the domain of attraction of a spectrally positive
\(\alpha\)-stable law.  More precisely, if \(a_n>0\) is chosen so that
\(n\Pr\{C>a_n\}\to1\), then for independent copies \(C_1,C_2,\ldots\),
\begin{equation}
 \frac{C_1+\cdots+C_n-n\mu_C}{a_n}
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm d}\mathcal S_\alpha,
 \label{eq:critical-cost-stable-domain}
\end{equation}
where the centered spectrally positive \(\alpha\)-stable law
\(\mathcal S_\alpha\) is fixed by the characteristic exponent
\begin{equation}
 \log\EE e^{it\mathcal S_\alpha}
 =\int_0^\infty
   (e^{itx}-1-itx)\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}\,dx.
 \label{eq:centered-stable-characteristic-exponent}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The critical equation \eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-at-one} makes the displayed
letter law a probability measure.  The local estimate
\eqref{eq:critical-letter-local-tail} and the context-sum evaluation in
\eqref{eq:critical-tail-constants} are \Cref{thm:arithmetic-denominator-layer}
at \(s=\sigma_0\).  Direct summation of that local estimate gives
\[
 \Pr\{C>x\}
 =\sum_{d>(x-1)/2}b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)
 \sim\frac{b_C}{\sigma_0-1}
      \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{1-\sigma_0},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:critical-letter-tail} with the stated \(K_C\).  Thus
regular variation is a conclusion of the arithmetic continuant estimate, not
an assumption.

Write \(\overline F(j)=\Pr\{C>j\}\).  The increments are nonnegative
integers, their mean \(\mu_C\) is finite because
\(\overline F(j)\sim K_Cj^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha>1\), and their span is
one: the fractions \(1/2\) and \(1/3\) give positive masses at costs (3)
and (5).  Thus all standing hypotheses of Omey--Van Gulck are satisfied.
The first displayed renewal asymptotic in
\cite[Sec.~3.2]{OmeyVanGulck2015} states, for an aperiodic nonnegative
integer law of finite mean and
\(\overline F\in RS(-\alpha)\), \(\alpha>1\), that
\begin{equation}
 u_j-\frac1\mu
 \sim\frac{j\overline F(j)}{\mu^2(\alpha-1)}.
 \label{eq:omey-van-gulck-renewal-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
Applying this displayed result with \(\mu=\mu_C\) and the proved tail gives
\[
 u_j-\frac1{\mu_C}
 \sim\frac{K_C}{\mu_C^2(\alpha-1)}j^{1-\alpha}.
\]
Substitution of \(\alpha=\sigma_0-1\) proves
\eqref{eq:critical-renewal-second-order}.  Summing it and using
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j^{2-\sigma_0}
 \sim\frac{m^{3-\sigma_0}}{3-\sigma_0}
\]
in the exact identities \eqref{eq:standard-layer-renewal} and
\eqref{eq:weighted-window-renewal} proves
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-second-order} and
\eqref{eq:finite-window-critical-second-order}; the boundary terms are
\(O(1)=o(m^{3-\sigma_0})\).

Finally, \eqref{eq:critical-letter-tail}, finite mean, and the absence of a
negative tail are precisely the one-sided domain-of-attraction conditions for
an \(\alpha\)-stable law with the normalization in
\eqref{eq:critical-cost-stable-domain}; see \cite[Ch.~XVII]{Feller1971}.
\end{proof}

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}

+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}

 \left(\sum_{a\ge h}a^{-s}\right)^2
 =O_s(h^{2-2s})=o(n^{-s}),
 \label{eq:two-large-digits-negligible}
\end{equation}
where the last equality is precisely the first inequality in
\eqref{eq:large-digit-cutoff}.

For words all of whose digits are smaller than \(h\),
\Cref{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound} applies.  When \(N\ge n/4\), its bound is
\(o(n^{-A})\) for every fixed \(A>0\), because \(n/h\to\infty\) and
\(\eta_s(h)\to0\).

The words not counted by \(P_n(s)\) and not covered by
\eqref{eq:two-large-digits-negligible} have at most one digit at least \(h\).
If there is none, apply \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound} with \(N=n\).  If
there is exactly one, its value is at most \(n/2\), so the two surrounding
moderate contexts have combined digit sum at least \(n/2\); one has digit sum
at least \(n/4\).  Cutting at the exceptional digit, bounding the short
context by \(L_s\), and allowing either context to be the long one gives the
explicit upper bound
\[
 2L_s\sum_{h\le a\le n/2}a^{-s}G_s(n/4,h).
\]
The first two factors grow at most polynomially, while the last is
superpolynomially small by \Cref{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}; hence this
is \(o(n^{-A})\) for every fixed \(A\).  Together with
\eqref{eq:two-large-digits-negligible}, this proves
\[
 A_n(s)-P_n(s)=o(n^{-s}).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:principal-large-digit-limit}, and replacing
\(n=d+1\) by \(d\), proves \eqref{eq:low-temperature-local-layer}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic critical stable renewal]
\label{thm:arithmetic-critical-stable-renewal}
Put \(\alpha:=\sigma_0-1\in(1,2)\), and under the critical letter law put
\[
 \Pr\{(C,H)=(c(p/q),\log q)\}=q^{-\sigma_0}.
\]
Then \(\Pr\{C=2d+1\}=b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)\), and the explicit constants
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 b_C&:=
 \sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
 \sum_{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}}
 \{\mathcal K(\mathbf u)\mathcal K(\mathbf v)\}^{-\sigma_0}
 =2\left(\frac{\zeta(\sigma_0-1)}{\zeta(\sigma_0)}\right)^2=8,\\
 K_C&:=\frac{2^{\sigma_0-1}}{\sigma_0-1}b_C
 =\frac{2^{\sigma_0+2}}{\sigma_0-1}
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:critical-tail-constants}
\end{equation}
are positive.  The double series defining \(b_C\) is absolutely convergent,
and
\begin{align}
 b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)&\sim b_Cd^{-\sigma_0},
 &&d\to\infty,
 \label{eq:critical-letter-local-tail}\\
 \Pr\{C>x\}
 &=\sum_{q\ge2}q^{-\sigma_0}
   \card{\{1\le p<q:(p,q)=1,\ c(p/q)>x\}},\notag\\
 &\sim K_Cx^{1-\sigma_0},
 &&x\to\infty.
 \label{eq:critical-letter-tail}
\end{align}
If \(u_j=u_j(\sigma_0)\) is the renewal sequence in
\eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-coefficients}, then
\begin{equation}
 u_j=\frac1{\mu_C}
 +\frac{K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)}j^{2-\sigma_0}
 +o(j^{2-\sigma_0}).
 \label{eq:critical-renewal-second-order}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 Z_m^R(-\sigma_0)
 &=\frac{2m}{\mu_C}
 +\frac{2K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)(3-\sigma_0)}
   m^{3-\sigma_0}+o(m^{3-\sigma_0}),
 \label{eq:standard-layer-critical-second-order}\\
 S_{-\sigma_0}(m)
 &=\frac{4m}{\mu_C}
 +\frac{4K_C}{\mu_C^2(\sigma_0-2)(3-\sigma_0)}
   m^{3-\sigma_0}+o(m^{3-\sigma_0}).
 \label{eq:finite-window-critical-second-order}
\end{align}
Finally, \(C\) belongs to the domain of attraction of a spectrally positive
\(\alpha\)-stable law.  More precisely, if \(a_n>0\) is chosen so that
\(n\Pr\{C>a_n\}\to1\), then for independent copies \(C_1,C_2,\ldots\),
\begin{equation}
 \frac{C_1+\cdots+C_n-n\mu_C}{a_n}
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm d}\mathcal S_\alpha,
 \label{eq:critical-cost-stable-domain}
\end{equation}
where the centered spectrally positive \(\alpha\)-stable law
\(\mathcal S_\alpha\) is fixed by the characteristic exponent
\begin{equation}
 \log\EE e^{it\mathcal S_\alpha}
 =\int_0^\infty
   (e^{itx}-1-itx)\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}\,dx.
 \label{eq:centered-stable-characteristic-exponent}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The critical equation \eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-at-one} makes the displayed
letter law a probability measure.  The local estimate
\eqref{eq:critical-letter-local-tail} and the context-sum evaluation in
\eqref{eq:critical-tail-constants} are \Cref{thm:arithmetic-denominator-layer}
at \(s=\sigma_0\).  Direct summation of that local estimate gives
\[
 \Pr\{C>x\}
 =\sum_{d>(x-1)/2}b_{2d+1}(\sigma_0)
 \sim\frac{b_C}{\sigma_0-1}
      \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{1-\sigma_0},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:critical-letter-tail} with the stated \(K_C\).  Thus
regular variation is a conclusion of the arithmetic continuant estimate, not
an assumption.

Write \(\overline F(j)=\Pr\{C>j\}\).  The increments are nonnegative
integers, their mean \(\mu_C\) is finite because
\(\overline F(j)\sim K_Cj^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha>1\), and their span is
one: the fractions \(1/2\) and \(1/3\) give positive masses at costs (3)
and (5).  Thus all standing hypotheses of Omey--Van Gulck are satisfied.
The first displayed renewal asymptotic in
\cite[Sec.~3.2]{OmeyVanGulck2015} states, for an aperiodic nonnegative
integer law of finite mean and
\(\overline F\in RS(-\alpha)\), \(\alpha>1\), that
\begin{equation}
 u_j-\frac1\mu
 \sim\frac{j\overline F(j)}{\mu^2(\alpha-1)}.
 \label{eq:omey-van-gulck-renewal-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
Applying this displayed result with \(\mu=\mu_C\) and the proved tail gives
\[
 u_j-\frac1{\mu_C}
 \sim\frac{K_C}{\mu_C^2(\alpha-1)}j^{1-\alpha}.
\]
Substitution of \(\alpha=\sigma_0-1\) proves
\eqref{eq:critical-renewal-second-order}.  Summing it and using
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j^{2-\sigma_0}
 \sim\frac{m^{3-\sigma_0}}{3-\sigma_0}
\]
in the exact identities \eqref{eq:standard-layer-renewal} and
\eqref{eq:weighted-window-renewal} proves
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-second-order} and
\eqref{eq:finite-window-critical-second-order}; the boundary terms are
\(O(1)=o(m^{3-\sigma_0})\).

Finally, \eqref{eq:critical-letter-tail}, finite mean, and the absence of a
negative tail are precisely the one-sided domain-of-attraction conditions for
an \(\alpha\)-stable law with the normalization in
\eqref{eq:critical-cost-stable-domain}; see \cite[Ch.~XVII]{Feller1971}.
\end{proof}

+\begin{proposition}[Exact identification with Dushistova's sum]
+\label{prop:dushistova-exact-identification}
+For \(n\ge2\) and \(\beta>1\), use Dushistova's conventions
+\[
+ \mathcal A_n^{\rm D}:=
+ \bigcup_{r\ge1}\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\mathbb N^r:
+ a_r\ge2,\ a_1+\cdots+a_r=n\},
+ \qquad
+ \sigma_\beta(n):=\sum_{\mathbf a\in\mathcal A_n^{\rm D}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf a)^{-2\beta}.
+\]
+Then, term by term,
+\begin{equation}
+ b_{2d+1}(s)=\sigma_{s/2}(d+1)
+ \qquad(d\ge1,\ s>2).
+ \label{eq:dushistova-exact-identification}
+\end{equation}
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Both sides are indexed by reduced fractions in \((0,1)\), but we spell out
+the convention change.  The canonical regular expansion of such a fraction
+is
+\[
+ [0;a_1,\ldots,a_t],\qquad a_i\ge1,\quad a_t\ge2,
+\]
+and its denominator is \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)\).  The elementary
+conversion to the unique negative expansion with digits at least two is, for
+even \(t\),
+\[
+ (a_1+1,2^{[a_2-1]},a_3+2,2^{[a_4-1]},\ldots,
+   a_{t-1}+2,2^{[a_t-1]}),
+\]
+where \(2^{[j]}\) denotes a string of \(j\) digits equal to two.  For odd
+\(t>1\), use the same alternating construction through \(a_{t-1}\), followed
+by \(a_t+1\); for \(t=1\), the negative word is \((a_1)\).  Induction in the
+continued-fraction recursions shows that the paired words represent the same
+fraction and hence have the same denominator.  Summing one less than each
+negative digit gives in all three cases
+\[
+ d(p/q)=a_1+\cdots+a_t-1.
+\]
+Thus \(c(p/q)=2d+1\) is equivalent to
+\((a_1,\ldots,a_t)\in\mathcal A_{d+1}^{\rm D}\), and the summand \(q^{-s}\)
+is exactly \(\mathcal K(a_1,\ldots,a_t)^{-s}\).  Dushistova's exponent is
+\(2\beta\), so \(s=2\beta\), proving the claimed termwise equality.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Endpoint correction in the left context]
+\label{lem:dushistova-endpoint-correction}
+For \(s>2\), put
+\[
+ r_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf v\in\mathcal C_{\rm R}\\
+                         |\mathbf v|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf v)^{-s},
+ \qquad
+ \ell_m(s):=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\
+                            |\mathbf u|_1=m}}
+          \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+ r_0=\ell_0=1,\qquad r_1=0,\qquad \ell_1=1,
+ \qquad \ell_m=2r_m\quad(m>1).
+\]
+Consequently, if
+\[
+ R_s:=\sum_{m\ge0}r_m(s)=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)},
+\]
+the three left-context cases contribute respectively
+\begin{equation}
+\begin{array}{c|c}
+ |\mathbf u|_1=0 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1=1 & R_s\\
+ |\mathbf u|_1>1 & 2(R_s-1)R_s
+\end{array}
+\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2R_s^2.
+\label{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}
+\end{equation}
+In particular, the conflicting printed and corrected coefficients are
+\begin{equation}
+ \boxed{\text{Dushistova: }R_s+2R_s^2}
+ \qquad\text{and}\qquad
+ \boxed{\text{this paper: }2R_s^2}.
+ \label{eq:dushistova-conflicting-constants}
+\end{equation}
+At \(s=\sigma_0\), these are \(10\) and \(8\), respectively.
+\end{lemma}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Canonical regular words of denominator \(q\) parameterize the
+\(\phi_{\rm E}(q)\) reduced fractions in \((0,1)\).  Including the empty word
+and using the totient Dirichlet series therefore gives the displayed value
+of \(R_s\), which is finite for \(s>2\).  For \(m>1\), every canonical word
+of digit sum \(m\) has exactly two positive expansions: itself and the word
+obtained by replacing its final digit \(a\ge2\) by \(a-1,1\).  This terminal
+move preserves both digit sum and continuant, so \(\ell_m=2r_m\).  At the two
+endpoints, however, the empty word is the only word of sum zero, while
+\((1)\) is the only positive word of sum one and is not canonical.  This
+proves all four identities and the three contributions in
+\eqref{eq:left-context-endpoint-cases}.
+
+The precise loss in the published argument occurs in the proof of
+Dushistova's Lemma~7 \cite[pp.~668--669]{Dushistova2007}.  After separating
+the \(u=1\) term, the proof replaces the \(u>1\) left-context sum by twice a
+canonical convolution denoted there by \(\Sigma_2\).  In the displayed
+definition of \(\Sigma_2\), the restriction \(u>1\) has disappeared, so the
+empty canonical context \(u=0\) is included; meanwhile the original \(u=0\)
+case is not retained separately.  Thus the printed split contributes
+\(R_s+2R_s^2\), an excess of exactly \(R_s\).  Retaining the three endpoint
+classes gives \(R_s+R_s+2(R_s-1)R_s=2R_s^2\).  This localization uses the
+same empty-continuant, final-digit, and exponent conventions as the published
+paper, so the discrepancy is not a normalization change.
+\end{proof}
+
+\begin{lemma}[Greedy moderate-block bound]
+\label{lem:greedy-moderate-block-bound}
+For \(s>2\), define
+\[
+ \eta_s(h):=
+ \sum_{\substack{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\\|\mathbf u|_1\ge h}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}
+\]
+and let \(G_s(N,h)\) be the total inverse-continuant weight of the words
+\(\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}\) with digit sum at least \(N\) and every
+digit smaller than \(h\).  For all sufficiently large \(h\),
+\begin{equation}
+ G_s(N,h)\le
+ \frac{L_s}{1-\eta_s(h)}
+ \eta_s(h)^{\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1},
+ \qquad L_s:=\sum_{\mathbf u\in\mathcal C_{\rm L}}
+ \mathcal K(\mathbf u)^{-s}=2R_s.
+ \label{eq:moderate-block-bound}
+\end{equation}
+\end{lemma}
+
 \begin{proof}
+Scan a word from the left and close a block at the first digit for which the
+block's digit sum reaches \(h\); repeat, leaving the final remainder unclosed.
+This greedy factorization is unique.  Since every digit is smaller than
+\(h\), each closed block has digit sum in \([h,2h)\), and a word of digit sum
+at least \(N\) has at least \(\lfloor N/(2h)\rfloor-1\) closed blocks.
+The concatenation inequality makes the inverse-continuant weight at most the
+product of the block weights.  The greedy map is injective into sequences of
+closed blocks and one remainder.  Enlarging each closed-block class to all
+positive words of digit sum at least \(h\) gives mass \(\eta_s(h)\), while
+enlarging the remainder class gives mass \(L_s\).  Summing the resulting
+geometric series proves \eqref{eq:moderate-block-bound}; it applies for large
+\(h\) because absolute convergence gives \(\eta_s(h)\to0\).
+\end{proof}
+
